summary: A brief list of RFCs through mid-May 1971, giving a title or partial title with its NIC and RFC numbers. It was a lookup aid for finding documents. It was replaced by later RFC lists, RFC 200 and RFC 999.

eli5.summary: A short index of all the notes so far, so you can find the one you want by its title and number.

how did people find early rfcs
subtitle: An early lookup guide for Request for Comments documents.

tldr.problem: By May 1971, the ARPA Network had accumulated more than 150 RFCs (Request for Comments documents), and there was no easy way to find a document if you knew its title but not its number.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 160 provides a brief list of RFCs organized by subject, showing each RFC's title (or partial title), its NIC (Network Information Center) catalog number, and its RFC number.
tldr.outcome: The brief list became a standard reference tool for the early networking community, quickly succeeded by more organized and comprehensive indexes as the RFC collection grew.

today: RFC 160 is Historic, superseded by RFC 170 and later by more comprehensive RFC indexes like RFC 200. It remains a snapshot of the early ARPA Network documentation effort.

sections.title: Finding Early RFCs
sections.content:
RFC 160 is a brief list of Request for Comments documents, giving a title or partial title for each RFC from 1 through 160. Each entry also includes the document's NIC (Network Information Center) catalog number, which was used to retrieve documents from the NIC's collection.

By May 1971, the early ARPA Network community had produced more than 150 RFCs covering network protocol design, implementation, meeting notes, and operational experience. A simple indexed list became essential for navigation.
sections.eli5: A short table listing all the notes written up to that point, so you could look one up by title.

sections.title: Contents and Organization
sections.content:
The list covers RFCs 1 through 160, organized by RFC number. Each entry shows the RFC's title, a reference to the NIC number for the original document, and the RFC number itself. Some RFCs were never formally numbered; these are noted as "not yet issued" or with no RFC assigned, allowing readers to distinguish formal RFCs from early proposal documents.

The notes indexed range from fundamental protocol work (HOST Software, Network Control Program) to meeting minutes, administrative documents, and late-breaking announcements. The titles are often abbreviated to fit the brief format.
sections.eli5: You could flip through this list, find the title you wanted, and see what number to ask for.

sections.title: Later Indexes
sections.content: RFC 160 itself appears in the list at its own location, documenting the rapid growth of the RFC collection. More comprehensive listings soon followed, including RFC 170 (RFC List by Number, adding author and date information) and later RFC 200 and 999, which superseded the brief list approach with more detailed and regularly updated indexes.
sections.eli5: This quick list was soon replaced by longer, more detailed ones that included more information about each note.

references.text: Network Information Center, "RFC List by Number", RFC 170, June 1971.
Postel, J. B., "ARPA Network Official Protocol", RFC 200, July 1971.
